name: Horn of Echeyakee
summary: The Horn of Echeyakee is a hunting instrument provided by Sergra Darkthorn at the Crossroads. Sounding it among the ancient kodo remains northeast of the settlement calls forth Whitemist, the legendary white predator of the Barrens.

sections.title: Calling the Whitemist
sections.body: Given to initiates testing their prowess in the hunt, the horn's call echoes across the savannah to summon Echeyakee, whose name translates from Taur-ahe as 'Whitemist.' Known as the king of the savannah cats, Echeyakee is revered by tauren hunters as both mercy and death, striking so swiftly that his quarry feels neither terror nor suffering. The horn is meant to be sounded only at the great predator's lair, a sun-bleached nest of giant kodo bones tucked behind the hills northeast of the Crossroads.

faq.q: What does the Horn of Echeyakee do?
aliases: what is horn of echeyakee for
faq.answer: The horn is used to draw out Echeyakee, the elusive white savannah cat. Blowing the horn near the giant kodo bones northeast of the Crossroads provokes the beast into appearing so a hunter may face him.

faq.q: Where does the horn come from?
faq.answer: Sergra Darkthorn, an orc huntress residing at the Crossroads in the Barrens, entrusts the horn to adventurers seeking to prove their subtlety and tracking skill.

faq.q: What does the name Echeyakee mean?
faq.answer: In the Tauren tongue of Taur-ahe, Echeyakee means 'Whitemist.' The name honors the beast's pale coat and his silent, mist-like ability to stalk through the dry grasses without being detected.

faq.q: Where do you blow the horn?
faq.answer: The horn must be sounded among the giant kodo ribs and skeletal remains found behind the hills northeast of the Crossroads, where the white lion makes his roaming ground.

angles.text: For hunters, summoning Echeyakee presents a legendary rite of passage, pitting their senses against a predator renowned across the Barrens for near-flawless stealth.
The hunt of Echeyakee carries spiritual weight among the tauren, who view the beast's swift, painless kill as an embodiment of both mercy and the harsh necessity of death.
